extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and educated general readers interested in the nature, value, and aesthetics of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for judging the merit, beauty, and significance of mathematical theorems and proofs (aimed at distinguishing 'real' mathematics from puzzles or trivialities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness / Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'serious' theorem is one which contains 'significant' ideas — ideas that influence thought beyond a narrow context and have deep repercussions in mathematics and sometimes outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness is evidenced by the theorem's influence (e.g., Euclid's and Pythagoras's theorems have influenced thought profoundly beyond mathematics). A serious theorem typically supplies material or concepts fundamental to larger structures (Euclid's theorem about primes supplies raw material for arithmetic). If a theorem lacks generality and depth conspicuously (as many isolated arithmetic curiosities do), it is unlikely to be serious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty / Aesthetic Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical patterns and theorems should be judged for beauty: an aesthetic quality combining unexpectedness, inevitability, and economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beautiful theorems/proofs often present surprising methods using simple tools, yet lead to inescapable conclusions. They avoid unnecessary complications and present one clear line of attack. The prose analogy: a proof should resemble a simple, clear-cut constellation rather than a scattered cluster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality (substantive, non-logical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea should be a constituent in many mathematical constructs, usable in proofs of many different theorems, capable of extension and typical of a class of theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generality here means the capacity for substantial extension and connection to many different ideas (not mere abstract universality). A useful test: can the special statement be extended or seen as representative of a broader phenomenon? Beware excessive generality which loses individuality and interest — the 'large generalization limited by a happy particularity' is fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth relates to how far down the 'strata' of mathematical ideas the theorem reaches; deeper ideas often lie in lower strata and are generally harder and more foundational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth is not identical to difficulty (some deep ideas are now easy to state), but deep theorems often require knowledge of lower strata or more powerful tools (e.g., Prime Number Theorem is deeper than Euclid's theorem because it requires analytic methods). Depth manifests when understanding or proving a result requires 'digging deeper' into foundational concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance / Economy of Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof should be economical and inevitable: using simple, often 'childishly simple' weapons to reach far-reaching results, with no escape from the conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer single-line, clear arguments over long enumerations of cases. Avoid proofs that rely on tedious casework; elegance often means one line of attack suffices and every step contributes meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Proof by Enumeration of Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive 'enumeration of cases' is considered a dull and inferior form of mathematical argument and detracts from a theorem's aesthetic and mathematical merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While variation and multiple replies are valuable in some problem genres (e.g., chess problems), in serious mathematics reliance on many similar case distinctions is looked down upon. Aesthetic preference is for unity and conceptual clarity rather than many repetitive variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-triviality / Freedom from Mere Curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem should not be an isolated arithmetical curiosity or a narrowly contrived fact with no broader connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples such as special numerical curiosities (unique reversal multiples, digit-cube sums) amuse amateurs but lack appeal to mathematicians because their proofs are uninteresting and not capable of generalization. A theorem's value increases when it connects to wider theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelessness / Freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Great theorems retain their freshness and significance across long spans of time; their statements and proofs remain striking even centuries after discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's and Pythagoras's theorems are cited as examples whose significance and beauty endure; a test of merit is whether the result still seems 'fresh and significant' long after discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness Combined with Inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic pleasure of a theorem often comes from the combination of a surprising approach and the sense that the conclusion was nonetheless unavoidable once seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that surprise by their form but leave the reader feeling there was no other possible route are highly prized. This quality contributes to both beauty and perceived depth/elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Utility (as one possible but not decisive value)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical usefulness of a theorem — whether it increases material well-being or has engineering/scientific application — is a criterion often considered but not definitive for judging mathematical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary mathematics (including calculus) has clear practical utility and is important for applications, but the 'real' mathematics prized for beauty and depth is often 'useless' in the crude practical sense. Utility can justify certain studies (e.g., to benefit society), but the absence of immediate application does not diminish aesthetic or theoretical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract Generality (logical/Whitehead sense) — not a discriminating criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: All mathematical theorems are equally 'general' in the abstract logical sense (statements about 'things' without regard to their nature); this kind of generality does not distinguish high-class theorems from trivial ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse mere abstract universality with the substantive generality that makes a theorem significant. Whitehead's notion of complete abstract generality is a truism and irrelevant for ranking the aesthetic or mathematical importance of theorems.
